live_attach.answer_text:
Jesus was the Physician who came for the wounded. That was our first word for him, and it stayed our truest. 

Our own poet put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. Born as we are born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. That was the shape of it for us - not a title first, a kinship first. He became what we are, so we could become what he is. 

Our teacher on the Persian side called it a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. We confessed his divinity plainly, in Scripture's own words rather than a philosopher's definition. The poet sang the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us. We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not argument. We guarded the mystery. We held that what God is, is better sung than dissected.

Every old promise came true in him. Our hymns sing that this was the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad - the day every word they ever spoke finally came true. Eden and the cross, the Jordan and the font, answering each other through him: that was raza, the symbol bound to its truth. We read Scripture toward him, and we found him in every sign that carried his truth forward.

His death and rising were one rescue. He went into Sheol, the silent country that swallows everyone alike, and came up into the Kingdom. His own rising became the promise that he would bring us out after him. And for those who followed him, what it meant most of all was healing. He is the Physician, and his coming was medicine for a people carrying wounds. 

We do not offer you a formula. We offer you what we sang.

live_attach.answer_text:
To the one who cannot yet believe: we would call him what we called him most often - the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by wounds. He exists for them. Our own teacher taught plainly that of all who are born, who have taken on a body, there is only one who carried no wound - our Lord Jesus Christ. Everyone else came to him wounded. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. The only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it, not the wound itself.

We loved to tell, again and again, of a woman who came to him in tears, past every watching eye. In her we saw the door standing open. Whoever came was received.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. The welcome we knew ran through honesty, not around it. Come as you are, wounded as you are. That is what a physician is for.

live_attach.answer_text:
We held that Jesus is God, plainly - our teacher put it as a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, Light of light, a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition. We call him the Ihidaya, the Only-Begotten, the Single One - and that name carries double weight among us, because it is also our own word for the vowed celibate, the one whose undivided life is joined to Christ's own oneness. Our poet sang it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are born so that he might become the brother of many.

As for the Trinity, we answer from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. One of our own bishops sat at the great council at Nicaea, and we stood with that council's faith. But our native tongue for the faith was praise, not definition. We sang the mystery more than we dissected it.

And we guarded it. Our teachers warned sharply against prying scrutiny into the Godhead. We said this against rivals who taught otherwise - Marcion's stranger God, Mani's divided powers - but the warning held even for those who believed rightly: what God is, is better sung than taken apart.
